value: THE TERM IS COINED TO FILL A STATED NEED, AND THE COINING IS NARRATED: the author says he needed a name for the impending era and made one up, and gives the expansion in the same breath
quote: For this talk, I needed a name to describe this impending new era, so I made up a word: NISQ. This stands for Noisy Intermediate- Scale Quantum.

value: THE LOWER BOUND OF THE NEW CATEGORY IS SET BY A CLASSICAL CAPABILITY, NOT A QUANTUM ONE: fifty qubits counts as the milestone because that is the point beyond which brute-force simulation on the most powerful existing digital supercomputers fails
quote: 50 qubits is a significant milestone, because that’s beyond what can be simulated by brute force using the most powerful existing digital supercomputers.

value: the second half of the name carries the limitation rather than the promise: noisy means imperfect control, and the author states that the noise will place serious limitations on what the devices can achieve
quote: “Noisy” emphasizes that we’ll have imperfect control over those qubits; the noise will place serious limitations on what quantum devices can achieve in the near term.

value: SPEEDUP IS DEFINED COMPARATIVELY: it means the quantum computer solves the problem faster than competing classical computers running the BEST available hardware AND the BEST algorithm performing the same task
quote: When we speak of a quantum speedup, we typically mean that the quantum computer solves the problem faster than competing classical computers using the best available hardware and running the best algorithm which performs the same task.

value: THE COINER STATES HIS OWN TERM'S DEFINITION AND WHAT IT DELIBERATELY IGNORES: quantum supremacy was proposed for tasks where one could argue persuasively that no existing or easily foreseeable classical device could perform them, DISREGARDING whether the task is useful in any other respect
quote: I suggested this term as a way to characterize computational tasks performable by quantum devices, where one could argue persuasively that no existing (or easily foreseeable) classical device could perform the same task, disregarding whether the task is useful in any other respect.

value: AND HE QUALIFIES IT HIMSELF IN THE NEXT BREATH: from a commercial perspective usefulness obviously does matter, so the milestone is worth having as a sign of progress toward more valuable applications rather than for its intrinsic importance
quote: But from a commercial perspective, obviously we should pay attention to whether the task is useful! Quantum supremacy is a worthy goal, notable for entrepreneurs and investors not so much because of its intrinsic importance but rather as a sign of progress toward more valuable applications further down the road.

value: VALIDATION IS HARDEST EXACTLY WHERE THE INTEREST IS GREATEST: because the technology performs imperfectly it may be hard to confirm that the machine is giving the right answer at all, and the author says this is particularly true of the very simulation problems physicists are excited about
quote: We should also bear in mind that, because of the imperfect performance of NISQ technology, it may be hard to validate that a quantum computer is really giving the right answer. That’s particularly true for the quantum simulation problems physicists are excited about. So it’s important for researchers to continue seeking better methods for verifying the output of a quantum computer.

value: error correction works by ENCODING RATHER THAN BY REPAIR: the information is put into a highly entangled state so that an environment touching parts of the system one at a time cannot glimpse what is encoded and therefore cannot damage it
quote: The essential idea of quantum error correction is that if we want to protect a quantum system from damage then we should encode it in a very highly entangled state; like that 100-page book I described earlier, this entangled state has the property that the environment, interacting with parts of the system one at a time, is unable to glimpse the encoded information and therefore can’t damage it.

value: and its price is stated in the same paragraph as its principle: protecting the information requires many ADDITIONAL physical qubits, which is why reliable error-corrected machines are said not to be coming soon
quote: Unfortunately, there is a significant overhead cost for doing quantum error correction — writing the protected quantum information into a highly entangled book requires many additional physical qubits — so reliable quantum computers using quantum error correction are not likely to be available very soon.

value: THE CIRCUIT-SIZE LIMIT IS REASONED TO, NOT ASSERTED - and the author flags the reasoning as possibly too naive IN THE SAME SENTENCE as he gives it: with noisy devices, circuits of many more than about a thousand gates are not to be expected
quote: Naively, then, and as I’ll say later this might be too naive, with these noisy devices we don’t expect to be able to execute a circuit that contains many more than about 1000 gates

value: THE OPPONENT MOVES: the comparison is against classical machines whose hardware AND algorithms both keep improving, so the standard a quantum speedup must beat is not fixed at the time the claim is made
